excerpt: Substack lets writers and creators publish newsletters, podcasts and video and charge for subscriptions, keeping 90% minus card fees. How it works, its funding and alternatives.
content:
Substack is a publishing platform for newsletters. A writer sets up a publication for free, sends posts by email and on the web, and can switch on paid subscriptions so that readers pay monthly or yearly for some or all posts. It has grown into podcasts, video, live streams, a Twitter-like feed called Notes, and a reader app where subscribers find new writers.

Substack was founded in 2017 by Chris Best, its chief executive, Hamish McKenzie and Jairaj Sethi. TechCrunch covered its launch in October 2017.

The business model is simple: publishing is free, and when a writer charges, Substack takes 10% of subscription revenue, with card processing fees on top.

In July 2025 Substack raised a $100 million Series C at a $1.1 billion valuation, led by BOND and The Chernin Group, with Andreessen Horowitz also taking part, Bloomberg and Axios reported. At the time it had more than 5 million paid subscriptions across the platform, Axios said, and more than 50 creators were earning over $1 million a year there.

We have not used Substack for this page. It brings together Substack's own website and pricing page and reporting from the outlets linked under Sources, and says where each fact comes from.

profile.starts_at: Free to publish; 10% of paid subscription revenue
profile.summary_short: Newsletter and subscription publishing platform for writers and creators

gallery.alt: Chris Best, later Substack's co-founder and CEO, giving a talk in 2015
gallery.credit: Photo: VMA Media, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

use_cases: Starting a free or paid email newsletter
Running a subscription podcast or video series
Building an audience through recommendations and Notes
Moving an existing mailing list to a paid model

fit: writers, journalists and analysts who want to be paid directly by readers
creators who want a free start with no monthly bill
people who want discovery from Substack's own network and app
not_fit: businesses sending marketing emails, which suit tools such as Mailchimp or Kit better
large paid newsletters, where a flat-fee platform may cost less than a 10% cut
publishers who want full control over design and their own website

pricing.intro: From Substack's going-paid page: publishing is free; on paid subscriptions writers keep 90% of revenue, minus credit card fees.

plans.name: Paid subscriptions
plans.detail: Writers set their own monthly and yearly prices

items.name: Medium
items.what: Publishing network with a paid membership
items.difference: Readers pay Medium, and writers earn from a shared pool, rather than charging their own subscribers.

items.name: Ghost
items.difference: Flat hosting fee and no revenue cut; can be self-hosted.

items.name: beehiiv
items.what: Newsletter platform with ads and growth tools
items.difference: Charges a subscription rather than a cut, with an ad network.

items.name: Kit (formerly ConvertKit)
items.difference: Strong automation for selling products by email.

pros: Free to start, with no monthly bill
Publishing, payments and email delivery handled in one place
Built-in discovery through recommendations, Notes and the app
cons: A 10% cut becomes expensive as revenue grows
Limited design control compared with your own website

faq.a: Yes, publishing is free. If you charge subscribers, Substack keeps 10% of that revenue and card fees are deducted too.
Chris Best, Hamish McKenzie and Jairaj Sethi founded Substack in 2017. Best is the CEO.
Its July 2025 Series C of $100 million valued it at $1.1 billion.

faq.q: How many people pay on Substack?
faq.a: Axios reported more than 5 million paid subscriptions across the platform in July 2025.
